passage: Lakshmi Ma'am had promised Bidisha "real training" when she joined the architecture firm in Pune. Six months on, Bidisha was drafting Lakshmi's client sheets until ten at night, collecting her dry cleaning, and watching her own name vanish from drawings, replaced by "Studio Lakshmi". On Saturday evening, on the balcony of her rented flat, she felt gratitude tugging against the knot in her stomach. On Monday morning she asked for ten minutes. "Ma'am, I would like to lead one drawing set myself, with my name on it. And I can't do personal errands in work hours anymore." Lakshmi said she was being ungrateful. Bidisha's hands shook, but she said she wanted to learn, and asked for an answer by month end. That night she also opened her CV.

qa.q: What did Bidisha ask for on Monday morning?
qa.a: To lead one drawing set herself with her name on it, and to stop doing personal errands in work hours.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha's hands shake as she made her request?
qa.a: Bidisha was nervous about challenging Lakshmi, torn between gratitude and loyalty on one side and a knot of unfairness about being used on the other.

qa.q: What could Bidisha do if the pattern continues after month end?
qa.a: Look for a firm that offers real training and fair credit, which she started by opening her CV.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi seem to see Bidisha's request?
qa.a: Lakshmi called Bidisha ungrateful, which suggests she took it as disloyalty rather than a fair ask.

grounding: A mentor uses a junior for free labour and credit under the name of guidance; the junior speaks up and prepares to leave if it continues.

passage:
I'm Aparna, the only woman in Pradeep sir's architecture studio, and for eight months I thought I was the lucky one.

He'd picked me as his mentee. "I'll teach you everything," he said. At first he did. Then the "learning" changed. I picked up his dry-cleaning. I booked his daughter's dance classes. I drew the full plans for the hospital wing, and at the client meeting he presented them as his, without my name.

I felt torn. He had opened doors for me. Maybe this was just how it worked? But every evening I went home angry, and I hadn't designed anything of my own in months.

One Monday I said it, as calmly as I could. "Sir, I'm grateful for your guidance. But I want the errands to stop, and I'd like my name on the hospital drawings. I'm here to learn design."

He looked offended. "Ungrateful." Two weeks later, nothing had changed. I applied elsewhere. I start at a new firm in June.

qa.q: What did Aparna pick up for Pradeep sir?
How did Aparna feel about the errands and the lost credit?
qa.a: Aparna felt torn between loyalty and unfairness, going home angry every evening.

qa.q: Why was leaving the right step for Aparna after speaking up?
qa.a: She had spoken up calmly and asked for fair learning and recognition, and when nothing changed, leaving stopped the exploitation.

qa.q: How did Pradeep sir see Aparna's request?
qa.a: Pradeep sir saw it as ingratitude, calling her "Ungrateful" instead of addressing the problem.

grounding: A first-person account shows a young woman whose mentor uses her for errands and takes credit for her work, who speaks up for fair learning and recognition and leaves when nothing changes.

passage:
University career office note, final-year counselling. Student: Eshaan, 23, research intern.

Eshaan came in exhausted. For six months he has worked in Dr. Ankita's lab "for experience": unpaid, weekends included. He showed me a conference paper: his analysis, her name first, his nowhere. He also does her grocery orders and collects her son from school.

He said, "She says this is how everyone learns. Maybe I'm being ungrateful." Then, more quietly, "But I haven't learned anything new since March."

I told him that feeling pulled between gratitude and a sense of unfairness is common in these situations, and that it is reasonable to expect real teaching and credit.

We planned a short conversation: thank her for the opportunity, ask for his name on the paper, ask to stop personal errands, and ask for one new skill to learn this term. If nothing changes in a month, we will look at other labs together.

Follow-up in two weeks.

qa.q: For how long has Eshaan worked in Dr. Ankita's lab?
qa.a: He has worked there for six months.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel about his work in the lab?
qa.a: Eshaan felt exhausted and torn, worrying he was ungrateful while feeling it was unfair.

qa.q: What plan did Eshaan and the career counsellor make?
qa.a: To thank Dr. Ankita, ask for his name on the paper, stop the personal errands, ask for new learning, and look at other labs if nothing changes.

qa.q: How does Dr. Ankita seem to see Eshaan's unpaid work?
qa.a: Dr. Ankita seems to see it as normal learning, saying this is how everyone learns.

grounding: A career counsellor's note shows a young man whose mentor uses him for free labour, credit and errands, who plans to speak up for fair learning and recognition and leave if the pattern continues.
